case_name: CASE OF ARVANITIS AND PHILELEFTHEROS PUBLIC COMPANY LIMITED v. CYPRUS

assessment.Existence of an interference and applica: The civil defamation judgment against the applicants, culminating in an award of EUR 12,000 plus interest, clearly amounted to an interference with their freedom of expression under Article 10 (see paragraphs 11 and 16). That interference was prescribed by law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation of others, so the central issue is whether it was “necessary in a democratic society”. In making that assessment, the Court usually examines whether the domestic courts struck a fair balance, applying criteria such as contribution to a debate of general interest, the status of the person concerned, the nature of the statements, the factual basis, the conduct of the journalist, and the severity of the sanction (see nos. 39954/08, 40660/08, 40454/07).

assessment.Debate of general interest: The impugned article concerned the recovery of Greek-Cypriot property from the occupied territories and the broader implications for the Cyprus problem, including litigation about property rights in the occupied areas (see paragraphs 6, 10 and 13). The domestic courts themselves accepted that this was a matter of public interest (see paragraph 13). Speech on such politically and historically sensitive matters attracts a high level of protection, and the margin of appreciation afforded to the State is correspondingly narrow (see no. 29369/10). This weighs strongly in favour of the applicants.

assessment.Status of C.K. and the permissible limit: Although the domestic courts characterised C.K. as a private individual rather than a public figure (see paragraphs 14 and 16), the Strasbourg approach is more nuanced. C.K. had voluntarily published an article in a prominent newspaper on a controversial public issue and was a lawyer involved in significant litigation concerning property in the occupied territories (see paragraphs 5, 6 and 12). Even if he was not a politician, he had entered the public arena on a question of general interest and could therefore be expected to display a greater degree of tolerance towards robust criticism than an ordinary private person unconnected with public debate (see nos. 39954/08, 40454/07, 29369/10). The domestic courts appear to have given insufficient weight to that factor.

assessment.Nature of the impugned statements: opini: The article was published as a signed column and was openly polemical in tone (see paragraph 6). Expressions such as “sell your dignity”, “hang your compatriots”, or references to “bargaining with thieves” were undoubtedly harsh and capable of offending. However, in context they appear largely as value judgments, rhetorical criticism and moral condemnation rather than precise factual accusations susceptible of strict proof. The Court consistently distinguishes between statements of fact and value judgments and accepts a degree of exaggeration and provocation in public-interest commentary (see nos. 29369/10, 17224/11, 60641/08). The domestic courts treated the article predominantly as a set of factual imputations, thereby narrowing the protection owed to opinion speech.

assessment.Whether there was a sufficient factual b: The key factual substratum of the article was not invented by the applicants. It derived from C.K.’s own published account: he had explained that he recovered one painting after paying money and the second by substituting a forgery, and he linked his conduct to the film The Thomas Crown Affair (see paragraphs 5 and 6). The applicants relied on that article and argued that their commentary was based on those undisputed facts (see paragraph 10). The domestic courts focused on semantic distinctions between “recovering” and “buying”, and on uncertainty as to whether the payment reached the holder of the painting or an intermediary (see paragraphs 12 and 16). Yet for Article 10 purposes, the question is not whether every pejorative formulation was literally exact, but whether the value judgments had a sufficient factual basis. Given C.K.’s own description of paying money to obtain a painting held in the occupied territories, the criticism had a tangible basis in fact. The domestic courts seem to have demanded an unduly high degree of proof for opinion-based commentary (see nos. 29369/10, 60641/08).

assessment.Good faith and journalistic duties: The District Court criticised the first applicant for not contacting C.K. before publication and inferred lack of good faith from that omission (see paragraphs 12 and 13). However, the first applicant was not reporting undisclosed allegations from anonymous sources; he was commenting on an article already published by C.K. himself (see paragraphs 5, 6 and 10). In such a setting, the duty of prior verification is less stringent than in investigative reporting, and the failure to seek comment cannot by itself justify a finding of bad faith. The applicants’ objective was to participate in an ongoing public debate and they relied on material already placed in the public domain by the person concerned (see paragraph 10). The domestic courts therefore appear to have applied an excessively rigid standard of journalistic conduct.

assessment.Balancing reputation against freedom of: C.K.’s reputation, including his professional standing as a lawyer, deserved protection (see paragraphs 9 and 12). Nevertheless, where criticism concerns conduct voluntarily disclosed by the person concerned and raises broader ethical and political implications, domestic courts must provide particularly relevant and sufficient reasons for restricting expression. Here, their reasoning rested mainly on the offensive tone of the article, the conclusion that C.K. was a private person, and a narrow reading of the factual basis (see paragraphs 12-16). They did not convincingly explain why robust criticism in the context of a newspaper column on a matter of public concern had to give way to reputation, especially given that the core facts came from C.K.’s own public account. The overall balancing exercise therefore appears deficient under the criteria developed in cases nos. 39954/08, 40660/08 and 40454/07.

assessment.Proportionality of the sanction and over: The sanction was civil rather than criminal, but EUR 12,000 plus interest is still capable of producing a chilling effect on the press, particularly in relation to commentary on matters of major public interest (see paragraph 11). Since the speech at issue lay close to the core of Article 10 protection, only especially weighty reasons could justify such liability. In the present case, the domestic courts’ reasons do not appear sufficiently relevant and sufficient. The article was a polemical value-laden response to C.K.’s own publication on an issue of undeniable public concern, and its factual basis was not absent. For these reasons, the most likely outcome is that the Court would find that the interference was not necessary in a democratic society and that Article 10 was violated.
